treatments.heading: Less invasive, often in our office
treatments.lede: Many treatments that once meant a hospital visit now happen in our offices, usually under local anesthesia, with most patients back to normal the same day.
items: Balloon sinuplasty
A small balloon gently widens blocked sinus openings, often without removing tissue or bone. Many people return to normal activities within 24 hours.
In-office sinus CT (MiniCAT)
An upright scanner made for sinuses and ears. Your doctor reviews the images with you in minutes, at 10 to 50 times less radiation than a standard head CT.
ClariFix cryotherapy
Cold therapy for chronic runny nose and congestion, 30–45 seconds per side. Most people improve within 2–6 weeks, with relief lasting up to two years.
LATERA implant
An absorbable implant that supports the side of the nose when weak cartilage collapses. 86% of patients reported better breathing.
PROPEL sinus implants
Placed during sinus surgery to keep openings clear and deliver anti-inflammatory medicine directly to the sinuses.
Tula ear tubes
Ear tubes placed in the office without general anesthesia, for children from six months and adults. The visit takes 30–45 minutes.
Inspire therapy
A mask-free implant for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea, for adults who have struggled with CPAP. A remote turns it on at bedtime.
BAHA bone-anchored hearing
A titanium implant behind the ear sends sound through bone to the inner ear, for conductive or mixed loss and single-sided deafness.
Videostroboscopy
Slow-motion video of your vocal cords as you speak, to diagnose hoarseness and other voice problems.
Septoplasty
Straightens the wall between the nostrils through small incisions inside the nose, with no visible scar. Most people go home the same day.

faq.question: How do I know if it’s sinusitis or just a bad cold?
faq.answer: A cold usually peaks in two to three days and improves within 10. Sinus symptoms tend to last beyond 10 days, or improve and then get worse again.

faq.question: Will I need surgery for my sinuses?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Most sinusitis is treated with medicines. Surgery is considered when chronic sinusitis doesn’t respond, or when polyps, a deviated septum or imaging show a structural cause.

faq.question: Can sinusitis cause tooth pain?
faq.answer: Yes. The roots of the upper back teeth sit right below the cheek sinuses, so inflamed sinuses can make those teeth ache.

faq.question: Is sinusitis contagious?
faq.answer: The cold virus that often starts it can be, but the sinus inflammation itself isn’t passed from person to person.

faq.question: Can I treat sinusitis at home?
faq.answer: Saline rinses, steam, fluids and decongestants help mild cases. If symptoms are severe, getting worse or lasting more than 10 days, see a doctor.

faq.question: Is a BAHA implant permanent?
faq.answer: It’s designed to last, but it can be removed if needed. The implant bonds with the bone behind the ear, and the sound processor is activated once it heals.

faq.question: Who is a candidate for Inspire therapy?
faq.answer: Adults 18 and over with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea who have tried and struggled with CPAP.

faq.question: What should I do about sudden hearing loss?
faq.answer: Treat rapid, unexplained hearing loss in one ear as an emergency. Contact us or go to an emergency room right away; early steroid treatment gives the best chance of recovery.

overview.heading: A full-service audiology and hearing aid practice
paras: SH Audiology has cared for hearing and balance since 1940. As part of SH Medical, we work alongside ENT, allergy, sleep, voice and physical therapy specialists, so your care connects.

Our mission is to go the extra mile: to care for you, and to explain the most innovative diagnostic and treatment technologies available. We stay involved in hearing and product development research, and our goal is simple: to optimize your hearing and make listening effortless.
We see adults and children, in person or online, and we want everyone to be able to hear the diverse sounds of our unique city.
overview.note: Audiologists hold a Doctor of Audiology (Au.D.) or a master’s degree, and are licensed to diagnose and treat hearing and balance disorders. They don’t perform surgery or prescribe medication; our ENT physicians do, in the same group.

conditions.heading: What we help with
conditions.lede: Hearing loss usually develops slowly, and on average people wait seven years before seeking treatment. The sooner it’s diagnosed, the more options you have.
items: Hearing loss
Signs include people seeming to mumble, trouble following group conversations or phone calls, and others remarking on your TV volume.
Types of hearing loss
Conductive (outer or middle ear), sensorineural (inner ear) or mixed, in one ear or both. The type and cause shape your plan.
Age-related hearing loss
Presbycusis affects about a third of adults over 65 and nearly half by 75. It usually comes on gradually, starting with high pitches.
Noise-induced hearing loss
The most common type in younger people. Sounds above 85 decibels can permanently damage the inner ear, but it’s usually preventable.
Tinnitus
Ringing, buzzing or pulsing in one or both ears. We help you manage it with hearing aids, sound therapy, counseling and retraining therapy.
Balance disorders
Dizziness, vertigo and unsteadiness, diagnosed with vestibular testing and treated with our balance and physical therapy team.
Auditory processing disorders
When the brain struggles to process sound and to tell speech apart from other noise.
Custom earmolds
Made from impressions of your ears for hearing protection and in-ear monitors: for musicians, swimmers, hunters and more.
Assistive listening devices
Portable amplifiers, on their own or with hearing aids and cochlear implants, that lift speech out of background noise.

treatments.heading: A complete picture of your hearing
treatments.lede: Quick and painless, usually with results the same day. After a physical exam and a look at your medical history, we use any of these tests.
items: Pure-tone testing
Through headphones in a sound-proof room, you signal when you hear tones of different pitch and volume. Results are charted on an audiogram.
Bone conduction testing
A small vibrator behind the ear sends sound straight to the inner ear, to tell conductive from sensorineural hearing loss.
Speech testing
Finds the faintest speech you can understand half the time, and how well you separate speech from background noise.
Tympanometry
Measures how your eardrum moves, to detect fluid, wax buildup, perforations and tumors in the middle ear.
Acoustic reflex testing
Measures involuntary muscle contractions in the middle ear to pinpoint where a hearing problem sits.
Auditory brainstem response
Records brainwave activity in response to sound. Also used to screen newborns.
Otoacoustic emissions
A tiny probe checks how the hair cells of the inner ear respond, looking for blockage, fluid or damage.
Online hearing test
A quick, free first step you can take at home before booking a full evaluation.

faq.question: What is the first sign of hearing loss?
faq.answer: Trouble understanding conversations in crowded places or on the phone, struggling to hear consonants, feeling tired after conversations, and ringing in the ears (tinnitus).

faq.question: How often should I have my hearing checked?
faq.answer: Healthy adults under 40 every three to five years. If you’re over 60, already have hearing loss or are regularly around loud noise, every year.

faq.question: Can hearing loss be restored?
faq.answer: Only in limited cases. Conductive loss can sometimes be treated with surgery or medicine. Sensorineural loss is permanent, but hearing aids can reconnect you with the sounds you’ve been missing.

faq.question: Will wearing a hearing aid make me look old?
faq.answer: Today’s hearing aids are small and discreet, and some are completely invisible. Asking people to repeat themselves is far more noticeable.

faq.question: Is it better to get hearing aids early?
faq.answer: Yes. Even mild untreated hearing loss is linked to a two to three times higher risk of falls in older adults, more listening fatigue and loneliness. Hearing aids help memory and social life.

faq.question: Do I need one hearing aid or two?
faq.answer: If only one ear has hearing loss, one aid. With loss in both ears, two help you hear in noise and tell where sounds come from.

faq.question: What is it like to hear through a hearing aid?
faq.answer: New sounds can seem loud or overwhelming at first while your brain adjusts. Follow-up visits help you settle in.

faq.question: What is an over-the-counter hearing aid?
faq.answer: An FDA-regulated device for adults with mild to moderate hearing loss that doesn’t need an exam or fitting. Prescription aids suit every level of hearing loss and are customized to you.

faq.question: What is a cochlear implant?
faq.answer: An electronic device that turns sound into digital signals sent to the brain, for people with severe or profound hearing loss who don’t benefit from hearing aids.

faq.question: Does tinnitus cause hearing loss?
faq.answer: No, though it can interfere with hearing. Many people with tinnitus also have hearing loss, because both can come from the same inner-ear conditions.

overview.heading: Care that builds lasting relationships
paras: Our physicians, medical assistants and patient care coordinators are committed to comprehensive, state-of-the-art care for allergies, asthma and immune conditions, and to partnering with you and your family for years to come.

Our allergists trained in internal medicine or pediatrics, then spent two to three more years specializing in allergy and immunology. We work closely with our ENT colleagues on sinus and nasal problems, and with your gastroenterologist on conditions like eosinophilic esophagitis.
glance: Medication testing and challenges, including penicillin
Patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis
overview.note: Allergists don’t treat brain fog, chronic fatigue, chemical sensitivity, dysautonomia, Ehlers-Danlos, POTS, dizziness, neuropathic pain, numbness or tingling, vertigo or hypertension, and we don’t offer testing for chemical sensitivity or mold toxicity.

conditions.heading: Allergies, asthma and the immune system
conditions.lede: An accurate diagnosis comes first: is it an allergy, and if so, what’s triggering it? Then we treat the cause as well as the symptoms.
items: Environmental allergies
Hay fever, allergic rhinitis and allergic conjunctivitis from pollen, dust mites, pets and mold, with testing and immunotherapy.
Asthma
From mild intermittent to severe persistent. In-office spirometry, inhalers, nebulizers, tablets and biologic injections.
Food allergies
History, skin or blood tests and supervised oral challenges. We help you spot cross-reactive foods and expand your diet when possible.
Eczema (atopic dermatitis)
Bathing routines, topical medicines, trigger avoidance and, for moderate to severe eczema from age 6, Dupixent.
Hives (urticaria)
Red, itchy welts that can disrupt sleep, school and work. Chronic hives often have no outside cause, and we help you control them.
Anaphylaxis
The most severe allergic reaction. We identify the cause so you can avoid future reactions, and make a plan with you.
Medication allergies
Standardized testing, including penicillin, with an oral challenge when needed to find out whether you’re truly allergic.
Insect sting allergies
Testing, an avoidance plan and venom immunotherapy, so you can still enjoy the outdoors.
Immunodeficiency
Recurrent infections can be a sign of one of over 300 primary immunodeficiencies. Treatment can include immunoglobulin replacement.
Angioedema
Swelling of the lips, eyes, throat or gut, often triggered by allergens, medicines or foods. We find the cause and lower the risk of it returning.
Eosinophilic esophagitis
Inflammation of the esophagus linked to food and environmental allergies, managed with your gastroenterologist.
Sinusitis and nasal polyps
Chronic sinus symptoms and polyps, treated with nasal or oral medicines, biologics and our ENT team.

treatments.heading: Treating the cause, not just the symptoms
treatments.lede: Most people start on more medicine to bring symptoms under control, then step down once things are stable.
items: Allergy shots (subcutaneous immunotherapy)
Regular injections that gradually train your immune system to tolerate your triggers, given at our five shot clinics.
Allergy tablets and drops
Sublingual immunotherapy you take at home, under the tongue.
Venom immunotherapy
Protection for people with serious reactions to insect stings.
Biologic medicines
Injections such as Xolair and Dupixent for severe asthma, nasal polyps, chronic hives and eczema when other treatments haven’t worked.
Inhalers and nebulizers
Reliever inhalers for symptoms, daily preventer inhalers to calm the airways, and nebulizers when inhalers are hard to use.
Asthma tablets
Leukotriene receptor antagonists, theophylline and, as a last resort, steroid tablets.
Immunoglobulin replacement
Intravenous or subcutaneous treatment for some immunodeficiencies.
Avoidance and diet plans
Practical steps to avoid triggers at home, and help reintroducing foods when it’s safe.

overview.heading: Testing, diagnosis and treatment made easy
paras: SH Sleep & Snoring is a sleep medicine clinic designed to make testing, diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders easy to reach across the Bay Area, from Sonoma to the South Bay, with several offices in San Francisco and remote options too.

Our team of nurse practitioners, board-certified otolaryngologists and board-certified sleep physicians offers evidence-based care. We don’t believe in one treatment for everyone; we work with you to find what fits your health, lifestyle and preferences.
glance: Loud snoring, or pauses in breathing that others notice
Gasping, choking or coughing at night
overview.note: Risk rises with a BMI over 30, high blood pressure that’s hard to control, a large neck, alcohol or sedatives, smoking, a family history, type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

conditions.heading: Snoring and sleep-related breathing
conditions.lede: In obstructive sleep apnea, relaxed muscles let the airway collapse during sleep. Oxygen can drop by 40% or more, and the brain wakes you briefly, sometimes hundreds of times a night.
items: Obstructive sleep apnea
The most common type, when soft tissue blocks the upper airway during sleep. Untreated, it strains the heart and blood pressure.
Snoring
About 45% of adults snore sometimes and 25% regularly. It’s caused by tissues vibrating as you breathe, and can be a sign of sleep apnea.
Central and complex sleep apnea
When the brain doesn’t send the right signals to breathe, alone or combined with obstruction.
Nasal obstruction
A deviated septum, enlarged turbinates or collapsing nasal valves that make breathing at night harder.
Enlarged tonsils and adenoids
A common cause of snoring and apnea, especially in children.
CPAP intolerance
If a mask hasn’t worked for you, there are other options, including oral appliances and Inspire therapy.

treatments.heading: Every option, available through us
treatments.lede: All of these treatments are available directly through SH Sleep & Snoring.
items: CPAP, AutoPAP and BiPAP
The gold standard for sleep apnea: a nightly machine that keeps your airway open for uninterrupted, restorative sleep.
Oral appliance therapy
A custom mouthpiece made by a dentist that holds your jaw forward. Effective for mild to moderate sleep apnea.
Weight loss and lifestyle coaching
Losing 10% of body weight can lower your apnea-hypopnea index by as much as 46%.
Nasal procedures
Turbinate reduction, nasal valve repair, septoplasty, sinus surgery and functional rhinoplasty, some in the office.
Throat procedures
Tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy, uvulectomy and UPPP to reduce crowding at the back of the throat.
Tongue reduction
A minimally invasive in-office radiofrequency treatment that firms the base of the tongue.
Inspire therapy

overview.heading: When the world won’t stay still
paras: A balance disorder makes you feel unsteady or dizzy. Even while standing, sitting or lying still, you may feel as if you’re moving, spinning or floating, and when you walk you may feel as if you’re tipping over.
It can come from anything that affects the inner ear or the brain, such as medications, ear infections or head injuries, and the risk rises as we get older.
Your inner ear works with your eyes, muscles and sense of touch to keep you balanced. Vestibular testing finds the weakest part of that system, so treatment can target it.
glance: Falling, or feeling you’re about to fall
Lightheadedness, faintness or a floating feeling
Nausea, vomiting, or changes in heart rate and blood pressure
overview.note: Even if your symptoms are mild today, they tend to worsen over time. Testing early makes the cause easier to treat.

conditions.heading: Conditions we care for
conditions.lede: We treat dizziness, vertigo and imbalance related to the inner ear and the brain, along with related joint and spine problems.
items: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
Brief, intense spinning triggered by certain head movements, when tiny crystals in the inner ear move into the balance canals.
Ménière’s disease
Vertigo, tinnitus, ear fullness and fluctuating hearing loss, usually in one ear, possibly from fluid buildup in the inner ear.
Labyrinthitis
Inflammation of the inner ear, usually from an infection, causing vertigo, temporary hearing loss and tinnitus.
Vestibular dysfunction
Problems in the inner ear’s balance system that cause dizziness, vertigo and unsteadiness.
Vestibular migraine
Migraine that brings dizziness or vertigo, with or without a headache.
Concussion and brain injury
Post-concussion syndrome and other brain injuries that affect balance, including sports concussion testing.
TMJ disorders
Pain and dysfunction in the jaw joint, which can also be linked to ear symptoms.
Spinal and orthopedic problems
Physical therapy for spine, joint and movement problems.

treatments.heading: Finding out why you feel unsteady
treatments.lede: Your ears play a key part in balance, so testing often covers hearing too. Depending on your symptoms, we may use:
items: Audiometry
Measures your ability to hear different sounds, pitches and frequencies.
Acoustic immittance measures
Evaluate the eardrum and middle ear to find which part of the ear is affected.
Auditory brainstem response
Records electrical activity along the hearing pathway between the inner ear and the brain.
Electronystagmography (ENG)
Electrodes around the eyes record involuntary eye movements that show how the vestibular system works.
Videonystagmography (VNG)
Tracks how your eyes respond to moving dots, head and body movements, and air or water in the ears.
Electrocochleography
An electrode in the ear measures the inner ear’s response to sound.
Otoacoustic emissions
A small probe checks how the hair cells of the inner ear respond.
Posturography
You stand on a platform while your posture and balance are measured under different conditions.
Sports concussion testing
The Balance Error Scoring System and the Sensory Organization Test help show whether an athlete has a concussion.

paras: Once we know what’s causing your symptoms, treatment targets that condition. Your plan may combine several of these.
bullets: Repositioning exercises for BPPV

Physical or occupational therapy
Medicines, such as antihistamines, sedatives, antibiotics or steroids

faq.question: I sometimes feel dizzy. Should I be tested?
faq.answer: Yes. Even if dizziness or vertigo hasn’t affected your life yet, it’s likely to worsen, and imbalance can become a safety concern. Finding the cause early makes it easier to treat or manage.

faq.question: Can I take my medication before vestibular testing?
faq.answer:
Some medicines change the results. Don’t take medicine prescribed for dizziness, and stop non-essential medicines for 48 hours. Keep taking medicines for blood pressure, heart or circulation problems and diabetes. Avoid:
- Anti-dizziness pills
- Sleeping pills and tranquilizers
- Antihistamines and over-the-counter cold or allergy medicines
- Narcotics
- Alcohol

faq.question: How do I prepare on the day?
faq.answer: Don’t eat or drink for three hours before the test, and don’t have caffeine, use tobacco, or wear makeup or face cream.

faq.question: How does the inner ear keep me balanced?
faq.answer: The inner ear has three parts. The cochlea handles hearing. The vestibule senses how much you’re moving forward and back, and the semicircular canals track where your head is in space.

specialists.title: Adult and Pediatric ENT Specialist / Head and Neck Surgeon
bio: Dr. Daniel Flis is a board-certified Otolaryngologist-Head and Neck Surgeon . He completed his residency in Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery in 2015. He completed a fellowship in Head and Neck Surgical Oncology and Endoscopic Skull Base Surgery at the University of California-San Francisco in 2016.

Dr. Daniel Flis treats a wide variety of adult and pediatric disorders of the head and neck. As a fellowship-trained head and neck cancer surgeon, his expertise includes treatment of benign and malignant tumors of the thyroid, salivary glands, oral cavity, oropharynx, sinonasal tract, skin, among other conditions of the head and neck.

specialists.name: Farshid Taghizadeh, MD
bio: Dr. Farshid Taghizadeh is a comprehensive otolaryngologist who cares for children and adults with a wide range of ear, nose, and throat conditions. His clinical interests include ear disorders, sinus and nasal obstruction, laryngology and voice concerns, sleep disorders, salivary gland disease, and general pediatric ENT care.

Dr. Taghizadeh is dedicated to building long-term, meaningful relationships with his patients and their families. He believes deeply in improving quality of life, and helping patients reach their fullest potential through both preventative and therapeutic care. His practice style emphasizes evidence-based medicine, shared decision-making, and understanding each patient’s individual goals and priorities.

Dr. Taghizadeh completed his medical degree and otolaryngology training at Oregon Health & Science University, where he was recognized with multiple awards for clinical excellence, research, and surgical skill. Having worked within healthcare systems in different countries and in diverse roles—from physical therapy to research—he brings a broad perspective and a commitment to accessible, culturally sensitive care. He is also passionate about integrating innovative, modern technology into ENT practice to enhance patient outcomes.
Outside of medicine, Dr. Taghizadeh enjoys spending time with his family, cooking, music, calligraphy, and hands-on projects. He is fluent in English and Farsi.

specialists.name: Angela L. Chang, MD
specialists.title: Board-Certified Allergist & Immunologist in San Francisco, CA
bio: Dr. Angela Chang is a board certified allergist and immunologist. She loves working with children and families and has interests in food allergy, eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis, and hives. She has been practicing allergy and immunology in the Bay Area since 2017 and is thrilled to join the San Francisco Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology group.

Dr. Chang earned her undergraduate degree at Duke University with B.S. in Biological Sciences. She earned her medical degree at Case Western Reserve University. She completed a residency in Pediatrics at Northwestern University and a fellowship in allergy and immunology at UCSF.
Dr. Chang is a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics; American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology; and the American College of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology.
In her free time, Dr. Chang enjoys spending time exploring San Francisco and eating sushi with her husband, daughter, son, and two pugs.

specialists.name: Stephanie Johannes, MD
specialists.title: Allergist & Immunologist in San Francisco, CA
bio: Dr. Stephanie Johannes is a board-certified allergist and immunologist in San Francisco, California. Dr. Johannes earned her medical degree at UCSF and completed residency in Pediatrics at Duke University. She completed fellowship in adult and pediatric Allergy and Immunology at the University of Colorado including training in cutting edge food allergy management at the Food Challenge and Research Unit at Children’s Hospital Colorado. Prior to medical training, Dr. Johannes earned a masters degree in molecular genetics and worked in translational immunology research at UCSF.

Dr. Johannes has a particular interest in working with infants, children, and families with food allergy, skin allergy, hives, eczema, and seasonal allergies. Additionally, she provides care for adults and children with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, and other allergic and immunologic disorders. Dr. Johannes emphasizes a collaborative approach, empowering patients to actively participate in their health and wellness. Outside of the clinic, Dr. Johannes loves biking, hiking, and traveling with her husband and three kids.

specialists.name: Conny Lu, MD
bio: Dr. Conny Lu is a board certified allergist and immunologist who strives to integrate evidence-based medicine with patients’ preferences, lifestyle, and goals. Her aim is to provide the highest quality of care across the spectrum of allergy and immunology for patients of all ages.

She earned her undergraduate degree in Biology from Washington University in St. Louis before returning home to New York City to obtain her medical degree at SUNY Downstate. Her training then brought her to the West Coast, where she completed a residency in Pediatrics at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles. Most recently, she completed a fellowship in Allergy and Immunology at UCSF.

Dr. Lu is thrilled to join the team at SH Medical. Her professional interests include allergic rhinitis, food allergy, eczema, asthma, and hives. Outside of medicine, she enjoys traveling, exploring new restaurants, and playing tennis.

specialists.name: Dean Kardassakis, MS, MD, FACAAI, FAAAAI
bio: Dr. Dean Kardassakis is a board-certified specialist in allergy, asthma, and immunology. He treats adults and children with several conditions including allergies involving the nose and eyes, asthma, atopic dermatitis (also called eczema), urticaria and angioedema (hives and swellings), food allergies, drug allergies, and recurrent infections.

Dean is a born and bred San Franciscan whose grandfather emigrated to San Francisco before the 1906 Earthquake. He attended U.C. Berkeley (Bachelor of Arts degree), Stanford University (Master of Science degree), and University of Nevada at Reno (Medical Degree and Residency in Internal Medicine). Dean completed his training with a two-year Fellowship in Allergy & Immunology at the University of California at San Francisco. He has worked in California ever since—with most of his time spent in San Mateo.

Dean has advanced to Fellowship in the American Board of Internal Medicine, the American College of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology, and the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology. He is a past president of the Northern California Allergy Association.
When he is not seeing patients or reading medical journals, Dean enjoys spending time with his wife and two dogs.

specialists.name: Steven Machtinger, MD
bio: Born in Brooklyn, New York, Dr. Steven Machtinger received his MD degree at the University of Pittsburgh before he and his wife, Karen, headed west. Following pediatric internship at the University of California, Irvine he served as a general practitioner on the Warm Springs Reservation in central Oregon. Dr. Machtinger completed residency in pediatrics and fellowship in allergy, immunology, and respiratory diseases at Stanford. Since completion of training, he has been in private practice in the San Mateo County. He is a past-president of the Western Society of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology and current president of the Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology Foundation of Northern California. He is a clinical adjunct associate professor at Stanford where he mentors fellows in allergy and immunology. Away from medicine he enjoys walking his corgi, playing guitar and spending quality time with his wife, son, daughter, and their families.

specialists.name: Terri Gallagher, Au.D.
bio: Terri Gallagher, Au.D., joined San Francisco Audiology in 1994, serving as its only audiologist for more than fifteen years. Dr. Gallagher specializes in diagnostic hearing evaluations and a complete spectrum of amplification options. Passionate about audiology, Dr. Gallagher has consistently been an advocate for the deaf and hard of hearing and an active participant in community health fairs and grand round lectures for various hospitals. She is also a member of various state and local audiology organizations. A San Francisco Bay Area native, Dr. Gallagher was awarded her B.A. and M.S. degrees from San Francisco State University and earned her Doctor of Audiology degree from Arizona School of Health Science.

specialists.name: Carey Philliposian, Au.D.
bio: Carey Philliposian, Au.D., joined San Francisco Audiology in October of 2014. Dr. Philliposian has been passionate about the field of audiology for more than 20 years, spending the past 17 years practicing adult and pediatric audiology in the Bay Area. Her experience ranges from private practice, non-profit and hospital settings such as UCSF Medical Center. In addition to being well versed in clinical audiology, her professional interests include audiology research and developing the San Francisco Audiology Research Center at San Francisco Audiology. Dr. Philliposian received her B.S. degree at the University of Washington, her M.S. degree from San Francisco State University and her Doctor of Audiology degree from Salus University, Pennsylvania. Being a native San Franciscan, Dr. Philliposian is thrilled to be working in the city that she loves.

specialists.name: Jeffrey Lampert, Au.D.
bio: Jeffrey Lampert, Au.D., joined San Francisco Audiology in April 2012. Dr. Lampert has more than 30 years of experience in the hearing healthcare field and is a member of the American Academy of Audiology and the California Academy of Audiology. Dr. Lampert earned his B.A. and Master of Audiology degrees from San Diego State University and his Doctor of Audiology from the Arizona School of Health Sciences (A.T. Still University). Prior to joining San Francisco Audiology Dr. Lampert worked in a number of otolaryngology practices and owned his own private audiology practice in San Mateo, California.

specialists.name: William Huson, Au.D.
bio: William Huson, Au.D., joined San Francisco Audiology at the start of 2017. After obtaining his B.A. in Linguistics and B.S. in Speech and Hearing Science from the University of Washington, he earned his Doctor of Audiology from the University of California–San Diego. Dr. Huson’s interests include the treatment of tinnitus, patient education and integrating the latest hearing aid technologies and research into his practice. With experience working in private practice, school districts and for major healthcare organizations, Dr. Huson enjoys delivering exceptional care to patients of all ages. To this day, Dr. Huson remains fascinated by hearing and language and is committed to helping every person reach their highest communication potential.

specialists.name: Nicole Schmidt, Au.D.
bio: Nicole Schmidt, Au.D. completed her bachelor’s degree in speech-language pathology and audiology from the University of Akron and obtained her Doctorate of Audiology from Central Michigan University. Her interests include vestibular diagnostics, tinnitus management and adult amplification. Dr. Schmidt focusses on evaluating each patient thoroughly to determine where the problem stems from to provide each patient the best possible outcome. She is a member of the American Academy of Audiology and American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. She is excited to join a team that focuses on exceptional patient care.

specialists.name: Jenna Cullinan, Au.D.
bio: Jenna Cullinan joined San Francisco Audiology in August 2022. Dr. Cullinan is a San Francisco native and is excited to be working in the city and the greater Bay Area. She received her B.A. in Communication Disorders and Sciences from the University of Oregon in 2018 and went on to obtain her Doctor of Audiology from the University of the Pacific in 2022. Dr. Cullinan’s interests include diagnostic hearing evaluations, patient education and amplification for pediatric and adult patients. She is passionate about audiology and providing high-quality hearing health care.

specialists.name: Rosana Amaro, Au.D.
bio: Rosana Amaro, Au.D., joined SH Audiology in October 2022. She was inspired to enter the field of audiology due to growing up with severe bilateral hearing loss, and her own experience with wearing hearing aids since early childhood. She completed her B.S. in Speech Language Pathology and Audiology from Towson University and her Doctorate of Audiology from University of the Pacific San Francisco. Dr. Amaro’s interests include diagnostic hearing evaluations, tinnitus management, and amplification for pediatrics and adults. She provides patient-centered care and advocates for the deaf and hard of hearing community.

specialists.name: Ana Tejeda, Au.D.
bio: Ana Tejeda, Au.D., joined San Francisco Audiology in October 2023. She is returning to San Francisco Audiology after finishing her doctorate in audiology at the University of the Pacific and working in multiple hospital settings. Dr. Tejeda’s expertise includes hearing aid dispensing, comprehensive hearing evaluations and balance testing. Her mission is to provide personalized care, helping individuals of all ages rediscover the joy of clear and balanced sound. Dr. Tejeda is committed to staying current with the latest audiology advancements to offer the best solutions to her patients.

specialists.name: Isabel Leyritana, Au.D.
bio: Isabel joined San Francisco Audiology in February 2025. Originally from the Philippines, she is a dedicated healthcare professional with over a decade of experience in both audiology and nursing. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Nursing and a master’s in clinical audiology from the University of Santo Tomas.

Her career in audiology began in 2013 in the Philippines, where she honed her clinical skills. She later expanded her expertise as a research assistant in the National University of Singapore’s M.Sc. Audiology program, focusing on hearing research in the elderly. After relocating to the United States, Isabel worked as a hearing aid dispenser while pursuing her Doctor of Audiology through Salus University’s Au.D. Bridge Program, earning her doctorate in 2021.

specialists.name: Hannah Torok, Au.D.
bio: Hannah Torok, Au.D., joined San Francisco Audiology in May 2024. She is a native Texan and received both her B.S. in Communication Sciences and Disorders and Doctorate of Audiology at the University of Texas at Austin. Dr. Torok has been living and working in the Bay Area since May 2022. Her expertise includes comprehensive hearing evaluations, patient education and hearing aid dispensing. She is excited to join our team and provide excellent patient care.

specialists.name: Chris Nicklo, HAD
bio: Chris Nicklo, HAD, joined San Francisco Audiology in 2018 after a career in business and marketing. Having worn hearing aids for twenty years, Chris knows firsthand how they can increase your confidence and make it easier to connect with family and friends. Chris received his Bachelor of Arts from Hampden-Sydney College in economics and French and his MBA from the University of Virginia’s Darden School of Business. He is a licensed hearing aid dispenser through the Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology and Hearing Aid Dispensers Board of California.

specialists.name: Robert Gilligan, HAD
bio: Robert Gilligan, HAD Joined San Francisco Audiology in May 2024. Robert grew up in New Zealand where he obtained his Masters of Audiology, and operates as a hearing aid dispenser in the US. Over his career he has worked in many different specialty areas, including neurodiagnostics, pediatrics and hearing aids. Most recently, he did a stint in hearing aid manufacturing.

specialists.name: Angela Smith, PT, MSPT
bio: Angela Smith has been a physical therapist since 1996. She completed her Bachelor of Science in health sciences and Master of Science in physical therapy at Boston University. Angela specializes in the treatment of dizziness, vertigo and imbalance related to vestibular dysfunction, vestibular migraines, post-concussion syndrome and other brain injuries. She treats TMJ as well as spinal and orthopedic dysfunction.
